title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Introduction
content: Natriuretic peptides are key proteins that improve and regulate circulation. These proteins are essential for acting on blood vessels, causing them to widen or dilate. [1] Natriuretic peptides are expressed predominantly by cardiomyocytes of the mixed secretory-contractile phenotype in atrial and ventricular walls. In addition to regulating blood pressure, natriuretic peptides inhibit cardiac hypertrophy and remodeling. [2] In patients with decompensated heart failure due to volume overload, a treatment-induced drop in wedge pressure is often accompanied by a rapid drop in natriuretic peptide levels. Measurement of natriuretic peptide levels may thus assist with hemodynamic assessment and subsequent treatment titration. [3] Natriuretic peptides can also be found in the kidneys and can cause the kidneys to excrete more water and salt. [4]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Introduction
content: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) was initially identified in porcine brain tissue in 1988 and was previously referred to as the brain natriuretic peptide. However, researchers later discovered that the primary site of BNP release is cardiac ventricular cells, particularly in response to ventricular distention. [5] Following this discovery, a substantial body of literature emerged regarding the use of BNP as a potential biomarker to measure the presence and severity of heart failure. [6]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Introduction
content: BNP is a member of the natriuretic peptide family that includes atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), C-type natriuretic peptide, D-type natriuretic peptide, and urodilatin. [7] ProBNP is a 108-amino acid precursor protein of BNP found in the ventricles and atria of the heart. Human ANP and BNP are encoded by genes located on chromosome 1. [8] In situations of volume overload and myocardial muscle stretching, proBNP is upregulated at the genomic level. [9]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Introduction
content: A small amount of BNP is found in the cytoplasmic granules of myocytes. Upon stimulation for production and release, proBNP is cleaved by corin to equimolar amounts of the biologically active BNP hormone and the biologically inactive amino-terminal proBNP (NT-proBNP), which is also released into circulation as the unprocessed precursor protein. [8] When evaluating its effects on vascular smooth muscle cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and myocytes, this peptide does not appear to have any biological activity. [10]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Introduction
content: C-type natriuretic peptide is primarily synthesized in the central nervous system. This peptide is also found in vascular endothelial cells and may play a role in the local regulation of vascular tone. [11] Unlike ANP and BNP, the human gene encoding CNP, NPPC , is not located on chromosome 1 but on chromosome 2. In normal human subjects, the mean concentration of CNP is very low (1 fmol/mL). [12] CNP levels are elevated in patients with heart failure, albeit to a much lower extent than ANP and BNP. The clearance of CNP-22 in human plasma is very rapid, with a calculated half-life of 2.6 minutes. [13]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Introduction
content: The natriuretic peptide system comprises 3 receptors—natriuretic peptide receptor-A (NPR-A), natriuretic peptide receptor-B (NPR-B), and natriuretic peptide receptor-C (NPR-C). [14] The human NPR-A gene is located on chromosome 1q21-22 and comprises 22 exons and 21 introns spanning approximately 16 kilobases. The human NPR-B gene is located on chromosome 9p12-21, and the murine version, Npr2 , is located on chromosome 4. The human NPR-C gene is located on chromosome 5p13-14 and contains 8 exons and 7 introns spanning more than 65 kilobases. [15] The natriuretic peptide receptors NPR-A and NPR-B catalyze the synthesis of a classic intracellular second messenger, cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). cGMP binds to proteins such as cGMP-dependent protein kinases, cGMP-binding phosphodiesterases, and cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels. [16] NPR-C controls the concentrations of natriuretic peptides through receptor-mediated internalization and degradation. An NPR-A to NPR-C ratio plays a role in regulating the biological activity of natriuretic peptides. [17]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Pathophysiology
content: BNP is a 32-amino acid peptide hormone with a molecular weight of 3472 Da. [6] The molecule consists of an N-terminal tail of 9 amino acids, a C-terminal tail of 6 amino acids, and a 17-member ring closed by a disulfide bond between 2 cysteine residues. Within this ring, 11 amino acids are conserved across the family of natriuretic peptides. [18] BNP binds to natriuretic peptide receptors A and C, leading to the loss of water and electrolytes, vasodilation, and inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis. [19] BNP is cleared from the circulation by neutral endopeptidases. The first 2 amino acids from the N-terminal sequence—serine and proline—are removed by dipeptidyl peptidase IV soon after BNP is released into circulation. [7]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Pathophysiology
content: Following systemic secretion, the natriuretic peptides activate transmembrane guanylate cyclases on the surface of endothelial cells, thereby increasing intracellular levels of cGMP, leading to vasodilation. Other systemic effects include diuresis and natriuresis, resulting in lowered blood pressure. [20] The peptides have also demonstrated the ability to antagonize adverse pathways that are over-activated in the setting of heart failure, for example, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, which has anti-diuretic effects, and the transforming growth factor-beta pathway, which increases cardiac remodeling and fibrosis. [21]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Pathophysiology
content: BNP gene expression is a feature of both atrial and ventricular myocytes. In a normal heart, the atrial regions are the primary site of BNP expression. Ventricular BNP gene expression increases drastically in cardiac diseases affecting the ventricles, such as heart failure. [22] Observing ventricular BNP gene expression in ventricular disease may have given rise to the common statement that BNP is predominantly a ventricular hormone. However, atrial and ventricular myocytes differ considerably in their endocrine phenotypes, and it is reasonable to expect significant differences in peptide storage and secretion patterns. [23] Atrial granules contain both intact precursors and biosynthetic end products, including bioactive ANP-28 and BNP-32. In contrast, normal ventricular myocytes do not seem to express such granules, and they do not contain proBNP-derived peptides. [24]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Pathophysiology
content: The estimated half-life of BNP is about 20 minutes, whereas NT-proBNP has a half-life of 120 minutes. This difference explains why NT-proBNP serum levels are approximately 6 times higher than BNP levels, even though both molecules are released in equimolar proportions. [25] Like BNP, NT-proBNP concentrations vary by age; the normal threshold for individuals younger than 50 is 450 pg/mL, whereas it is 900 pg/mL for those older than 50. [26] The clinical importance of measuring one peptide over the other has not yet been demonstrated.

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Pathophysiology
content: BNP production in cardiomyocytes is significantly increased by inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1-beta, an effect that is markedly increased when fibroblasts are present. These inflammatory cytokines directly stimulate BNP production in the heart independent of hemodynamics. [27] This phenomenon is not observed with ANP. In clinical practice, plasma BNP levels are higher in patients with myocarditis than expected solely from the hemodynamics. [28]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Specimen Requirements and Procedure
content: BNP is labile and should be collected in EDTA-containing tubes, ideally tested within 4 hours of collection. Serum samples and citrated or heparinized plasma can not be used. BNP can be stored at 2 °C to 8 °C for up to 24 hours for certain assays. [29] BNP is degraded by contact activation of the blood coagulation system and can be stabilized by storage under frozen conditions or by adding kallikrein protease inhibitors. [30] In contrast, NT-proBNP is much more stable than BNP and can be kept at refrigerated temperatures for 3 days. NT-proBNP can be tested in serum and plasma collected in either heparin or EDTA. When EDTA plasma is used, the NT-proBNP concentration is about 10% lower than for serum or lithium heparin. [31]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Testing Procedures
content: Both BNP and NT-proBNP levels can be tested through standard blood draws. [32] BNP and NT-proBNP are determined by several different immunoassays using antibodies directed to different epitopes on the antigen molecules. title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Interfering Factors
content: BNP and NT-proBNP levels may be affected by specific comorbidities, such as chronic renal failure, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and acute coronary syndrome. [23] Levels are higher in patients with renal failure, diabetes mellitus, and acute coronary syndrome, and lower in patients with obesity. [7] Decreasing renal function with age may be partly responsible for the increase in BNP/NT-proBNP. In the absence of heart failure, the concentration of BNP/NT-proBNP increases in patients with a decreasing glomerular filtration rate. [35] Older individuals who appear healthy may have declining cardiac function not detectable by current noninvasive techniques. [36]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Interfering Factors
content: The body mass index (BMI) is another variable influencing the reference intervals for BNP and NT-proBNP. Patients with a BMI in the obese range have lower BNP and NT-proBNP concentrations compared to those with a normal or underweight BMI. Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain this phenomenon. [37] Natriuretic peptide receptors are highly concentrated in adipose tissues, suggesting that BNP is likely degraded there. However, this does not account for the obesity effect observed for NT-proBNP, which is not degraded by these receptors. [38] Therefore, comparisons of levels among patients are less meaningful than tracking the peptide trajectory of an individual patient. [39]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Interfering Factors
content: All immunoassays for BNP and NT-proBNP are heterogeneous, using a separation step between bound and free antibodies; there are no problems with photometric interferents such as hemoglobin, bilirubin, or lipemia. [40] The cross-reactivity of assays for BNP and NT-proBNP towards proBNP is an important consideration since it is now known that proBNP also circulates in the blood of patients with heart failure. [41] Because proBNP is the precursor protein to both BNP and NT-proBNP, the epitopes used to raise antibodies for these latter 2 peptides are also present in the proBNP peptide structure. [42]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Interfering Factors
content: ProBNP also exists in the blood of patients with heart failure as an O-linked glycoprotein. There are 7 potential glycosylation sites from the center of the molecule (from the non-BNP amino acid sequences). [43] Several studies have tested the cross-reactivity of proBNP towards commercial BNP and NT-proBNP assays. For BNP, the cross-reactivity ranged from 17% to 38% for glycosylated proBNP and 5% to 14% for non-glycosylated proBNP. [44] For NT-proBNP, the cross-reactivity ranged from 29% to 249% for non-glycosylated proBNP, but with no cross-reactivity towards glycosylated proBNP. [45]

[46] Therefore, comparing the results of different markers and different assays of the same marker is difficult. [8] The clinical significance of the presence of human anti-mouse antibodies and heterophile antibodies is diminished for BNP and NT-proBNP assays; mild false-positive results do not have significant clinical implications. [47]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings
content: BNP and NT-proBNP levels increase in patients with cardiac disease due to myocardial stress and volume overload. [42] Patients with a BNP elevation of over 100 pg/mL should be assessed further for the signs and symptoms of cardiac disease. [48] Although BNP is traditionally used in the diagnosis of left ventricular systolic function, it can be elevated through other conditions, including right ventricular failure, acute myocardial infarction, congenital heart disease, and valvular disease. [6]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings
content: Other conditions in which natriuretic peptides are elevated include any disease that increases blood volume and wall stress, such as sepsis, anemia, renal dysfunction, Cushing syndrome, hyperaldosteronism, hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy, and cirrhosis. [49] In healthy individuals, BNP levels vary by age and genetic sex; levels increase with age and are higher, on average, in females than in males. [34]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings
content: Circulating levels of natriuretic peptides increase after acute myocardial infarction; the extent of the increase is related to the size of the infarct. [50] Patients with smaller infarcts tend to have a monophasic increase in plasma BNP levels, peaking 20 hours after the onset of symptoms. In contrast, patients with larger infarcts, lower ejection fraction, and clinical signs of heart failure may present a further peak 5 days after admission. [51]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Results, Reporting, and Critical Findings
content: A BNP value of less than 100 pg/mL and an NT-proBNP level of less than 300 pg/mL makes the diagnosis of heart failure less likely in patients with acute dyspnea. [52] Elevated levels of natriuretic peptides are associated with poor long-term prognosis and have an adverse impact on long-term mortality in patients with heart failure and various other conditions, such as coronary artery disease and atrial fibrillation. [53]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Clinical Significance -- Heart Failure
content: The primary indication for BNP measurement is distinguishing between cardiogenic and noncardiogenic causes of dyspnea in an emergent setting. Dyspnea is a symptom in nearly all cases of heart failure exacerbation. However, it is not specific to heart failure and may result from other pathological processes. [54] The sensitivity of BNP in heart failure is approximately 97%. Therefore, a normal BNP level (<100 pg/mL) effectively rules out heart failure and should prompt a search for noncardiac causes of dyspnea. An elevated level may indicate the presence of cardiac disease and the need for further cardiac workup, such as echocardiography, to determine the etiology of the patient's symptoms. [32] Furthermore, short-term elevations in hospitalized patients with heart failure have correlated with longer hospital stays.

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Clinical Significance -- Heart Failure
content: BNP can also be a useful prognostic marker in patients with known chronic heart failure; elevated levels are found in patients with higher New York Heart Association functional class scores and correlate with mortality, morbidity, and recurrent hospital admission. [20] [55] Furthermore, in hospitalized patients with heart failure, short-term elevations in BNP have been shown to predict increased hospital stays. [56]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Clinical Significance -- Acute Coronary Syndrome
content: Left ventricular dysfunction due to cardiac remodeling is a significant cause of mortality following myocardial infarction. BNP monitoring can help assess prognosis following myocardial infarction, as elevated levels are associated with post-myocardial infarction left ventricular dysfunction with ejection fractions less than 40%. [57]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Clinical Significance -- Limitations
content: Although BNP is a useful tool in assessing prognosis in patients with cardiac disease, it has not been well established that BNP-guided therapy offers improved outcomes compared to symptom-guided therapies. [54] Therefore, knowledge of BNP levels may predict outcomes but does not yet dictate treatment in the chronic management of heart failure. For this reason, BNP should not be used as a stand-alone test when guiding therapy in cardiac disease. Furthermore, although elevated BNP levels are highly sensitive to heart failure, they are not specific to its cause; elevated BNP levels may be observed in various cardiac and noncardiac diseases, as previously mentioned. Therefore, evaluating abnormal BNP levels with further cardiac testing is necessary. [57] Particular care is needed when interpreting an elevated BNP in patients with multiple comorbidities, such as those with renal failure, to identify the cause of the elevation. [19]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Clinical Significance -- Relevance
content: Heart failure is a significant and growing cause of morbidity and mortality in the United States; it is the leading cause of hospitalization in individuals aged 65 or older and is responsible for 10% of all healthcare expenditures. [56] Many symptoms of heart failure exacerbations are not specific to the disease process; therefore, identifying a biomarker that could assist in the diagnosis process was critical. BNP measurement is a highly sensitive, low-cost, and rapid test that can be used in hospitals to assist in diagnosing heart failure. [58]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: For non-waived tests, laboratories are expected to perform analysis of a minimum of 2 levels of control materials every 24 hours. If necessary, laboratories can assay quality control (QC) samples more frequently to ensure accurate results. QC samples should be assayed after calibration or maintenance of an analyzer to verify the correct method performance. [59] To minimize QC when performing tests for which manufacturers' recommendations are less than those required by the regulatory agency—such as once per month—laboratories can develop an individualized QC plan that involves performing a risk assessment of potential sources of error in all phases of testing and putting in place a QC plan to reduce the likelihood of errors. [60]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Quality Control and Lab Safety
content: All specimens, control materials, and calibrator materials should be considered potentially infectious. The usual precautions required for handling all laboratory reagents should be exercised. Disposal of all waste material should be in accordance with local guidelines. Gloves, a lab coat, and safety glasses should be worn when handling human blood specimens. All plastic tips, sample cups, and gloves that come into contact with blood should be placed in a biohazard waste container. [62] All disposable glassware should be discarded into sharps waste containers. All work surfaces should be protected with disposable absorbent bench-top paper, which should be discarded into biohazard waste containers weekly or whenever blood contamination occurs. All work surfaces should be wiped weekly. [63]

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The effective interpretation and application of BNP testing relies on a collaborative interprofessional approach. Clinicians and advanced practice providers are responsible for interpreting BNP results within the broader clinical context to support prompt diagnosis and management, especially for heart failure and acute cardiac events. Nurses play a role in identifying early symptoms, facilitating timely testing, monitoring patient responses, and providing patient education. Pharmacists contribute by optimizing heart failure therapies based on BNP trends and evaluating medications for potential interactions or necessary adjustments.

title: Natriuretic Peptide B Type Test -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Clear communication among all team members is essential for consistent interpretation and coordinated care planning. Responsible and strategic use of BNP testing supports both laboratory stewardship and equitable patient care. Effective care coordination is critical in emergency and transitional care settings, aiding in triage, admission, and discharge decisions. When BNP testing is properly integrated into clinical workflows, it enhances diagnostic accuracy, patient safety, and the effectiveness of the cardiovascular care team as a whole.
